concepts.name: Origins and Institutional Architecture of the Green Revolution
key_dimensions: Role of Norman Borlaug, Ford Foundation, and Rockefeller Foundation vs. Indian scientists like M.S. Swaminathan — attribution trap
Establishment of IARI, ICAR, and their mandates vs. international bodies like CIMMYT
Policy context: transition from PL-480 dependence to food self-sufficiency as a political driver
UPSC trap: distinguishing 'Green Revolution' from 'Gene Revolution' and 'Evergreen Revolution' (Swaminathan's concept)

concepts.name: High-Yielding Variety (HYV) Seeds: Characteristics and Limitations
key_dimensions: Dwarf wheat varieties (Lerma Rojo, Sonora-64) and rice varieties (IR-8 'Miracle Rice') — specific names often tested
Why HYVs are input-responsive but NOT input-independent — a critical conceptual distinction
Genetic uniformity of HYVs leading to vulnerability to pests/diseases (Irish Potato Famine analogy)
UPSC trap: HYV seeds require MORE water, fertilizer, and pesticides — they did NOT reduce input dependency

concepts.name: Geographical Spread: First-Phase Concentration (Punjab–Haryana–Western UP Belt)
key_dimensions: Why this belt was selected: flat terrain, canal irrigation (Bhakra-Nangal), relatively consolidated landholdings
Agro-climatic suitability vs. deliberate policy choice — causes of regional concentration
Exclusion of rain-fed, arid, and tribal regions — creating a 'Green Revolution island'
UPSC trap: Bihar and Eastern UP had similar soil but were excluded due to poor infrastructure — not agro-climatic reasons

concepts.name: Crop-Specific Nature: Wheat-Centric First Phase vs. Rice in Second Phase
key_dimensions: First Green Revolution (1960s–70s): predominantly wheat in northwest India
Second Green Revolution attempt: extending to rice in parts of Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu (Cauvery delta), and Punjab
Crops left out: pulses, oilseeds, coarse cereals (millets, sorghum) — the 'neglected crops' narrative
UPSC trap: India became self-sufficient in wheat BEFORE rice — sequencing matters for prelims

concepts.name: The 'Package Programme' Approach: Technological vs. Institutional Bundle
key_dimensions: Intensive Agricultural District Programme (IADP, 1960) and Intensive Agricultural Area Programme (IAAP) as precursors
Components: HYV seeds + chemical fertilizers + irrigation + credit + market linkage — all must work together
Why it failed to replicate in rain-fed areas: the package is indivisible — removing one component collapses the system
Comparison with HYVP (High Yielding Varieties Programme, 1966–67) as the formal launch

concepts.name: Role of Irrigation Infrastructure in Enabling the Green Revolution
key_dimensions: Tubewell revolution in Punjab-Haryana: groundwater exploitation enabled expansion beyond canal commands
Canal irrigation (Bhakra-Nangal, Upper Ganga Canal) vs. groundwater — sustainability contrast
Groundwater depletion in Punjab as a long-term consequence — water table falling >1 meter/year in some areas
UPSC trap: Green Revolution increased irrigation dependency, making agriculture MORE vulnerable to groundwater depletion, not less

concepts.name: Inter-Regional Inequality: States That Benefited vs. States Left Behind
key_dimensions: Gainers: Punjab, Haryana, Western UP; Partial gainers: AP, Tamil Nadu; Left behind: Bihar, Odisha, NE India, dryland Deccan
Regional disparity in agricultural productivity as a lasting legacy — Green Revolution widened the gap
The 'spread effect' failure: why technology did not diffuse to eastern India despite fertile soil (Gangetic plains paradox)
Policy debates: whether extension of Green Revolution to eastern India (e.g., 'Bringing Green Revolution to Eastern India' scheme, 2010) succeeded

concepts.name: Intra-Regional Inequality: Large Farmers vs. Small/Marginal Farmers
key_dimensions: Capital-intensive technology favored farmers with access to credit, land, and irrigation — widening rural class divide
Displacement of sharecroppers and tenants as land became more valuable — reverse tenancy
Green Revolution and the rise of the 'bullock capitalist' class in Punjab-Haryana
UPSC trap: Green Revolution increased production but ALSO increased inequality — candidates must hold both truths simultaneously

concepts.name: Impact on Food Security and Caloric Availability
key_dimensions: National food grain production: ~50 MT (1950) → ~100 MT (1968) → ~200 MT (1990s) — trajectory matters
Buffer stock creation and the Public Distribution System (PDS) — Green Revolution enabled PDS expansion
From 'ship-to-mouth' existence (PL-480 dependence) to food security: a sovereignty narrative
UPSC trap: Green Revolution ensured caloric (carbohydrate) security but NOT nutritional security — protein/micronutrient deficits persisted

concepts.name: Ecological and Environmental Consequences
key_dimensions: Soil degradation: waterlogging and salinity in canal-irrigated areas; micronutrient depletion (zinc, sulfur deficiency)
Chemical overuse: Punjab has highest pesticide use per hectare in India — 'cancer train' (Bathinda–Bikaner Express) controversy
Monoculture replacing diverse cropping systems — loss of agrobiodiversity (traditional varieties going extinct)
Groundwater contamination with nitrates and pesticides — linking Green Revolution to health outcomes

concepts.name: Agrarian Distress in Post-Green Revolution Punjab: The Paradox of Prosperity
key_dimensions: Declining farm profitability despite high productivity — cost-price squeeze as input costs rose faster than MSP
Paddy-wheat monoculture trap: farmers locked into two crops due to MSP/procurement policy, depleting water and soil
Farm debt, suicide, and social consequences — comparing Punjab's crisis with Vidarbha (different causes, same outcome)
UPSC trap: Punjab's distress is NOT due to low productivity but due to structural/policy failures post-Green Revolution

concepts.name: Green Revolution and the Minimum Support Price (MSP)–Procurement Nexus
key_dimensions: MSP as an incentive mechanism that drove Green Revolution adoption — the policy-technology complementarity
Selective procurement (wheat, rice) distorting cropping patterns away from pulses and oilseeds
How MSP for paddy in Punjab encouraged water-intensive rice cultivation in a semi-arid state
UPSC trap: MSP exists for 23 crops, but effective procurement happens mainly for wheat and rice — this is a major policy distortion

concepts.name: Green Revolution's Impact on Employment and Rural Labour
key_dimensions: Short-term positive employment effect: higher cropping intensity, multiple cropping cycles increased labor demand
Medium-term negative effect: mechanization (tractors, harvesters) displaced agricultural labor — Green Revolution → mechanization link
Migration dynamics: Green Revolution attracted migrant labor to Punjab from Bihar/UP while also displacing local labor
Gender dimension: feminization of agriculture in Punjab as men moved to non-farm work, but women's land rights didn't improve

concepts.name: Second Green Revolution: Concept, Targets, and Criticism
key_dimensions: Targeting rain-fed areas, eastern India, dryland Deccan, and neglected crops (pulses, oilseeds, millets)
Evergreen Revolution (M.S. Swaminathan) vs. Second Green Revolution — philosophical distinction: productivity without ecological harm
National Food Security Mission (NFSM) and Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) as policy instruments
UPSC trap: 'Second Green Revolution' is NOT an official government scheme — it's a policy vision; candidates confuse it with specific programmes

concepts.name: Biotechnology and GM Crops as the 'Gene Revolution': Continuity or Departure?
key_dimensions: Bt Cotton (2002) as India's first approved GM crop — impact on cotton yield and pesticide use in Vidarbha, Telangana
Bt Brinjal controversy: GEAC approval vs. moratorium (2010) — science-policy conflict
GM crops debate: food security vs. biosafety, corporate control of seeds (Monsanto/Bayer), farmer autonomy
UPSC trap: Bt Cotton is the ONLY commercially approved GM crop in India — all others (HT Mustard pending) are under moratorium as of knowledge cutoff

concepts.name: Green Revolution and Cropping Pattern Shifts: Diversification vs. Monoculturization
key_dimensions: Pre-Green Revolution: diverse cropping (mixed farming, millets, pulses) vs. post-Green Revolution: wheat-rice dominance
Punjab converting traditional 'kharif maize + rabi wheat' system to 'kharif paddy + rabi wheat' — an ecologically inappropriate shift
Loss of traditional varieties: thousands of rice landraces replaced by IR-8 and its derivatives
Policy efforts at diversification: Punjab government's incentives to shift away from paddy — largely unsuccessful

concepts.name: Green Revolution, Federalism, and Centre-State Agricultural Policy
key_dimensions: Agriculture is a State subject (List II) — Centre could only incentivize, not mandate, Green Revolution adoption
APMC Acts (state-level) and their role in ensuring procurement — how state-level institutions enabled or blocked Green Revolution
Why some states (Bihar, pre-2006) had poor adoption: weak state institutions, poor infrastructure, fragmented land holdings
UPSC trap: Centre's role in Green Revolution was through Planning Commission, ICAR, and price support — NOT direct administration

concepts.name: Social and Political Consequences: Green Revolution and the Punjab Crisis (1980s)
key_dimensions: Economic prosperity + regional neglect + Akali political mobilization → linkage to Punjab insurgency (contested but debated)
Rising aspirations of prosperous farmer class and political alienation — Green Revolution created a politically assertive peasantry
Demand for Satluj-Yamuna Link (SYL) Canal as a resource conflict directly tied to Green Revolution water politics
UPSC trap: causal relationship between Green Revolution and Punjab insurgency is DEBATED — candidates must present multiple perspectives, not assert causation

concepts.name: Nutritional Security Gap: Green Revolution's Blind Spot
key_dimensions: Caloric sufficiency achieved but protein deficiency (pulse production stagnated), micronutrient deficiency ('hidden hunger') worsened
Per capita pulse availability FELL from ~60g/day (1960s) to ~35g/day (2000s) — a direct consequence of policy bias toward wheat/rice
Biofortification (e.g., iron-rich pearl millet, zinc-rich wheat) as a corrective strategy under ongoing programmes
UPSC trap: India's malnutrition paradox — food surplus coexists with malnutrition; Green Revolution is a key explanatory variable

concepts.name: International Comparisons: Green Revolution in Asia — India vs. Other Countries
key_dimensions: Philippines, Indonesia, Bangladesh: similar HYV adoption but different outcomes — institutional context matters
China's agricultural transformation: collectivization → decollectivization (1978) vs. India's Green Revolution path — a contrast UPSC may use
Sub-Saharan Africa: why Green Revolution didn't replicate there — soil heterogeneity, infrastructure deficit, seed system failure (Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa/AGRA critique)
UPSC trap: Green Revolution is often presented as a universal model, but its replicability is highly context-dependent — candidates must know the conditions that enabled it
